title: E.J. Waggoner and the Abrahamic Covenant: God's Everlasting Promise
description: An exploration of E.J. Waggoner's revolutionary interpretation of the Abrahamic covenant, emphasizing righteousness by faith, unilateral divine grace, and the universal scope of God's promise to bless all nations through Christ, challenging prevailing conditional understandings of salvation.

waggoner_faith_before_works.name: Faith Before Works: Genesis 15 vs 17
waggoner_faith_before_works.introduction: Waggoner's foundational insight centered on the chronological and theological precedence of Abraham's justification by faith in Genesis 15 over the institution of circumcision in Genesis 17. This sequence established that righteousness comes through belief, not ritual performance.

paragraphs.heading: Abraham Believed and Was Justified
paragraphs.content: In Genesis 15:6, 'Abraham believed in the Lord; and He counted it to him for righteousness.' For Waggoner, this was the pivotal moment of justification, occurring through faith alone. Abraham's act of belief was like saying 'Amen' to God's word, building upon God's promise as a 'sure foundation.' This righteousness was not theoretical but 'an actual fact' that brought transformation both 'inside and outside' the man.

paragraphs.heading: The Unilateral Covenant Ratification
paragraphs.content: The covenant ratification in Genesis 15 demonstrated God's exclusive responsibility for its fulfillment. Only God, represented by 'a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch,' passed between the divided pieces while Abraham slept. This act signified that God alone guaranteed the covenant, making it unilateral and unconditional. For Waggoner, this represented the 'purely Gospel' aspect of God's dealing with humanity.

paragraphs.heading: Circumcision Comes Later
paragraphs.content: Circumcision was not instituted until Genesis 17, years after Abraham's justification. Waggoner emphasized that circumcision was 'a sign or seal of the righteousness of the faith which he had yet being uncircumcised' (Romans 4:11). This chronology proved that faith and righteousness precede any outward sign or ritual requirement. The sign confirmed what already existed, rather than creating righteousness.

paragraphs.heading: The Everlasting Nature of the Promise
paragraphs.content: Waggoner identified this Abrahamic covenant as 'the everlasting covenant,' representing God's unchanging plan of salvation. This covenant was confirmed by God's own oath, making it immutable and demonstrating that salvation is 'wholly of God.' The gospel was 'as full and complete in the days of Abraham as it has ever been or ever will be,' requiring no addition or change after God's oath to Abraham.

waggoner_circumcision_seal.name: Circumcision as Seal, Not Source
waggoner_circumcision_seal.introduction: Rather than viewing circumcision as a prerequisite for righteousness, Waggoner understood it as a divine seal confirming an already-existing faith. This reframing emphasized the spiritual over the ceremonial, pointing to an inward transformation of the heart.

paragraphs.heading: A Seal of Existing Righteousness
paragraphs.content: Waggoner taught that circumcision 'brought nothing to its possessor' but served as a 'token of the possession of such righteousness' already received through faith. It was an assurance that Abraham was 'accepted in the Beloved.' The sign had no power to create righteousness but only to confirm what God had already granted through Abraham's belief.

paragraphs.heading: Memorial of Human Inability
paragraphs.content: The sign's primary purpose was to remind Abraham and his descendants of their prior 'mistake' with Hagar in Genesis 16, where Abraham attempted to achieve God's promise 'by the flesh.' Circumcision warned against self-reliance, emphasizing that the promise was 'not to be gained by the flesh, but by the Spirit.' The cutting off of flesh symbolized that divine promises cannot be fulfilled through human effort.

paragraphs.heading: Circumcision of the Heart
paragraphs.content: True circumcision, according to Waggoner, was spiritual—'circumcision of the heart.' This meant having 'no confidence in the flesh' and worshipping 'God in the Spirit.' It signified 'complete distrust of self, and confidence and rejoicing in Christ Jesus.' This inward reality was what the outward sign was meant to represent, emphasizing character transformation over ritual compliance.

paragraphs.heading: A False Sign Without Faith
paragraphs.content: Waggoner warned that circumcision became 'a false sign unless the righteousness of faith was in the heart.' Later generations perverted this sign, assuming that mere possession of it assured their righteousness 'whether they kept the law or not.' This led them to trust in their own righteousness rather than understanding circumcision's true object: teaching them 'not to put confidence in themselves.'

waggoner_universal_blessing.name: Universal Blessing: All Nations Through Christ
waggoner_universal_blessing.introduction: Waggoner's interpretation of Genesis 12:3 emphasized the universal scope of God's promise to bless 'all the families of the earth' through Abraham. This blessing, fundamentally spiritual and Christ-centered, transcended national boundaries and offered salvation to every individual through faith.

paragraphs.heading: The Promise to All Families
paragraphs.content: In Genesis 12:3, God promised that 'in thee shall all the families of the earth be blessed.' Waggoner identified this blessing as 'the forgiveness of sins,' available only 'through the cross of Christ.' This promise was inherently spiritual and eternal in nature, encompassing people of all nations and demonstrating God's universal love and impartiality.

paragraphs.heading: Christ as the True Seed
paragraphs.content: The 'seed' of Abraham, according to Waggoner, was primarily Christ, and by extension, all who are 'Christ's' become Abraham's 'seed' and heirs according to the promise. This interpretation broadened the covenant beyond ethnic boundaries, making it accessible to anyone who accepts Christ by faith. The prophecy pointed to 'a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues.'

paragraphs.heading: God's Missionary Purpose
paragraphs.content: Waggoner argued that God's original design for Israel was to be a 'missionary people,' making His law and name known to all nations. God's desire for all people to know Him was equal to His desire for Israel to know Him. He chose Israel not out of favoritism, but because they were 'nearer at hand' to reveal Himself to others. This established the universal mission of redemption from the beginning.

paragraphs.heading: True Israel Defined by Faith
paragraphs.content: For Waggoner, 'To be an Israelite indeed, therefore, is simply to be a Christian.' Anyone who accepts Christ, regardless of nationality, 'ceases to be a Gentile, and becomes a member of the commonwealth of Israel.' Conversely, anyone 'without Christ,' whether Jew or Gentile, is 'without God' and 'a stranger from the covenants of promise.' This truth applies to people in all ages, making faith the sole criterion for covenant membership.

waggoner_promise_vs_law.name: Promise vs Law: The Galatians 3 Framework
waggoner_promise_vs_law.introduction: Waggoner's interpretation of Galatians 3 established the chronological and theological precedence of God's promise to Abraham over the Mosaic law. The law, given 430 years later, served not to provide salvation but to reveal sin and drive humanity to Christ.

paragraphs.heading: The 430-Year Gap
paragraphs.content: Paul's argument in Galatians 3 emphasized that the law was given 430 years after God's promise to Abraham. For Waggoner, this chronological gap proved that the law could not 'disannul' or alter the terms of the Abrahamic covenant. The promise was established first and remained unchanged, demonstrating that salvation was always by faith, not by law-keeping.

paragraphs.heading: Why Was the Law Added?
paragraphs.content: The law 'was added because of transgression,' Waggoner taught, meaning it was given to make sin abound and create conviction of sin. Its purpose was not to offer an alternative path to righteousness but to expose humanity's utter inability to achieve justification through their own efforts. The law became a 'ministration of death' when approached through human works because 'by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified.'

paragraphs.heading: The Law Points to Christ
paragraphs.content: Rather than providing salvation, the Sinaitic covenant 'contained no provisions for pardon of sins.' Forgiveness was always obtained 'by virtue of the promised sacrifice of Christ,' the Mediator of the new covenant. The law's role was to drive sinners to seek freedom in Christ, who is the true source of righteousness and the 'Living Law.' This made the law a schoolmaster to bring people to Christ.

paragraphs.heading: The Law in the Promise
paragraphs.content: Waggoner maintained that the law itself was in the Abrahamic covenant from the beginning, but its public proclamation at Sinai served to underscore its 'awful importance' and the 'terrible nature of sin.' This exposure of sin was intended to 'drive the sinner to seek freedom' in Christ. The law described God's character, and through faith, this character would be imprinted upon the heart, enabling genuine obedience.

waggoner_unilateral_grace.name: Unilateral Grace: God's Unconditional Promise
waggoner_unilateral_grace.introduction: Central to Waggoner's theology was the understanding that the Abrahamic covenant represented God's unilateral and unconditional promise of salvation. This covenant was not bilateral, requiring human performance, but was guaranteed entirely by God's own oath and character.

paragraphs.heading: God's Oath Confirms the Promise
paragraphs.content: The Abrahamic covenant was confirmed by God's own oath, making it 'immutable' and an 'end of all strife.' Waggoner emphasized that God 'sware by Himself' to Abraham because He could swear by no one greater. This divine oath underscored God's sole responsibility for the covenant's fulfillment, removing any human conditional element from its establishment.

paragraphs.heading: The Promise, Not Our Promise
paragraphs.content: Waggoner consistently taught that the covenant was 'the promise of God to save us, not our promise to obey Him.' This distinguished it fundamentally from the Sinaitic covenant, where the people promised to obey ('All that the Lord hath spoken we will do'). The Abrahamic covenant was entirely God's initiative and guarantee, making salvation 'wholly of God' rather than dependent on human performance.

paragraphs.heading: Only God Passed Through
paragraphs.content: In the covenant ratification ceremony of Genesis 15, only God, represented by 'a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch,' passed between the divided animal pieces. Abraham was in a deep sleep and took no active part in the ratification. This symbolized that God alone took responsibility for fulfilling every aspect of the covenant, making it unilateral and unconditional.

paragraphs.heading: All Promises Yes in Christ
paragraphs.content: For Waggoner, 'all the promises of God in Him [Christ] are Yes, and in Him Amen.' Every promise was given through Christ and found its fulfillment in Him. This meant the Abrahamic covenant was inherently Christocentric, with Christ as both the means and the guarantee of its fulfillment. The covenant's spiritual and eternal nature was secured by Christ's work, not human effort.

waggoner_sabbath_covenant.name: Condition vs Time: Two Covenant Attitudes
waggoner_sabbath_covenant.introduction: Waggoner revolutionized covenant understanding by teaching that the distinction between old and new covenants was not temporal but attitudinal. The difference lay in human response—self-effort versus faith in God's promises—rather than historical dispensations.

paragraphs.heading: Not Matters of Time, But Condition
paragraphs.content: Waggoner's fundamental insight was that 'the two covenants are not matters of time, but of condition.' This challenged the common view that distinguished the old covenant as valid before Christ and the new covenant as coming into effect afterward. Instead, the distinction was based on human attitude: the old covenant represented self-reliance and human promises, while the new covenant represented faith and reliance on God's promises.

paragraphs.heading: The Old Covenant Attitude
paragraphs.content: The old covenant, exemplified at Sinai, was characterized by the people's promise to obey: 'All that the Lord hath spoken we will do.' This was 'a virtual promise to make themselves righteous,' attempted without divine help. This covenant 'contained no provisions for pardon of sins' and became a 'ministration of death' because it relied on human effort to achieve righteousness, which is impossible due to human sinfulness.

paragraphs.heading: The New Covenant Reality
paragraphs.content: The new covenant, identical to the everlasting Abrahamic covenant, was God's promise to write His law in the heart and provide forgiveness of sins. This covenant existed 'in every feature long before the first, even from the days of Adam.' It represented God's unilateral work of transformation, where righteousness comes through the indwelling Christ, enabling genuine obedience as a result of salvation, not as a means to earn it.

paragraphs.heading: The Sabbath in Abraham's Covenant
paragraphs.content: Waggoner taught that the Sabbath was 'in the covenant made with Abraham' and was part of the righteousness of faith long before Sinai. True Sabbath-keeping was not a work for salvation but 'the absolute rest that comes from perfect faith in the power of God to create a new man and keep the soul from falling into sin.' It represented cessation from self-effort and trust in God's creative and sanctifying power, making it a sign of faith rather than a burden of law.
